system.name: Recipe sharing web app
system.description: Users publish recipes, browse, comment, and upload photos. 100 registered users, 2 developers, GBP 50/month infrastructure budget, no stated availability target, no stated compliance requirements.

functional: Register, authenticate, and manage an account
Publish a recipe with title, ingredients, method, and tags
Upload one or more photos per recipe
Browse and search recipes by text, ingredient, and tag
Edit and delete own recipes and comments

non_functional.name: recovery point objective (RPO)
non_functional.value: unstated; design targets 5 minutes or better via point-in-time recovery

non_functional.name: recovery time objective (RTO)
non_functional.value: unstated; must be established by a measured restore test, not assumed

assumptions.text: 30% of registered users are daily active
assumptions.impact: Roughly +/-3x on RPS. At 10% it is 0.009 req/s peak; at 100% it is 0.93 req/s peak. Neither changes any component.

assumptions.text: 2 sessions per active user per day, 40 requests per session (image-heavy browsing)
assumptions.impact: Linear on RPS and egress. Even 3 sessions of 60 requests gives 4.2 req/s peak, still one instance.

assumptions.text: Peak factor of 10, from the single-timezone consumer traffic shape; a cooking app concentrates around late afternoon and evening
assumptions.impact: Direct multiplier on provisioning. At 20x it is 0.56 req/s, still 5% of a conservative single-instance capacity.

assumptions.text: 95% reads / 5% writes; browsing dominates publishing and commenting
assumptions.impact: Sets write rate at 0.014/s. Any relational database handles this; the ratio would have to invert by three orders of magnitude to matter.

assumptions.text: 200 recipes published per month across all users, at 3 photos each: 600 photos/month, 20 photos/day
assumptions.impact: Drives object storage growth and async job volume. At 10x it is 230 GB/year of storage and 200 jobs/day, both still comfortable.

assumptions.text: Photos are 3 MB originals from phone cameras; served derivatives are ~200 KB web-size and ~30 KB thumbnail
assumptions.impact: Dominates both storage growth and egress. Halving served sizes halves egress; egress is negligible either way at this volume.

assumptions.text: Recipes and their photos are public; there is no per-user access control on media
assumptions.impact: If media must be private, derivatives cannot be served with public-read object URLs and every image needs a short-lived signed URL. That is application work, not a new component.

assumptions.text: Audience is single-timezone (UK), consistent with a GBP budget
assumptions.impact: Sets the peak factor and rules out multi-region. A globally distributed audience would raise the latency question, not the capacity one.

assumptions.text: The two developers have previously operated a managed relational database and a managed application platform
assumptions.impact: If false, the unfamiliar_technology modifier adds 1 point per unfamiliar component and the design goes over budget immediately.

assumptions.text: User-published recipes and photos are irreplaceable; losing them is a total failure regardless of the system's size
assumptions.impact: Makes tested backups, point-in-time recovery and object versioning unconditional rather than proportional to traffic.

assumptions.text: The application platform can run a scheduled task from the same codebase and deployment as the web process, without billing a separate always-on process
assumptions.impact: If the platform requires a separate always-on worker, that is +1 point and the design is 5/4 - over budget. Verify before choosing the platform.

assumptions.text: The smallest managed relational plan provides automated backup with point-in-time recovery, not snapshot-only backups
assumptions.impact: Snapshot-only means an RPO of up to 24 hours instead of minutes. This is a plan-selection criterion, not an architecture change.

assumptions.text: No compliance constraints, as none were stated
assumptions.impact: If the audience is in the UK or EU, data protection law applies to stored email addresses and user content regardless of what was stated. The architectural consequence is small - a working account-and-content deletion path that also removes objects from storage - but it is not zero.

assumptions.text: A single small managed application instance sustains at least 10 requests/second for this workload
assumptions.impact: This is the load-bearing assumption behind rejecting a load balancer and a second instance. It is deliberately conservative and is the first thing to measure. It sets the 2,500-user revisit trigger.

assumptions.name: dau_share
assumptions.impact_if_wrong: +/-3x on RPS

assumptions.name: sessions_per_day
assumptions.impact_if_wrong: linear on RPS

assumptions.name: requests_per_session
assumptions.impact_if_wrong: linear on RPS

assumptions.name: peak_factor
assumptions.impact_if_wrong: direct multiplier on the provisioning number only

results.formula: requests_per_day = users * dau_share * sessions_per_day * requests_per_session ; avg_rps = requests_per_day / 86400 ; peak_rps = avg_rps * peak_factor

safety_margin.rationale: The capacity-planning defaults apply 2x headroom on top of any assumed traffic shape, because the peak factor is the least reliable input in the chain. Provisioning target is therefore 0.56 requests/second. This changes no component.

sensitivity.explanation: At the low extreme (10% daily active, 1 session of 20 requests, 4x peak) this is 0.0093 req/s. At the high extreme (100% daily active, 3 sessions of 60 requests, 20x peak) it is 4.2 req/s. That is a 450x range, and every point in it is under half of a conservatively-assumed 10 req/s single-instance capacity. The recommendation does not change anywhere in the plausible input range.

notes: Computed from the documented formulas in calculators/README.md; python3 execution was unavailable in this environment, so the calculator was not run.
Read/write split of 95/5 gives 0.27 reads/second and 0.014 writes/second at peak.

assumptions.name: photos_per_day
assumptions.impact_if_wrong: linear on object storage growth

assumptions.name: bytes_per_photo_retained
assumptions.impact_if_wrong: linear; dominated by the 3 MB original

assumptions.name: index_overhead
assumptions.impact_if_wrong: none - object storage has no index or page overhead, so the relational default of 2.5 does not apply here

results.formula: bytes_per_day = photos_per_day * bytes_per_photo * index_overhead ; bytes_per_year = bytes_per_day * 365
results.calculation: bytes_per_day = 20 * 3.23 MB * 1.0 = 64.6 MB ; bytes_per_year = 64.6 * 365 = 23579 MB = 23 GB

sensitivity.explanation: At 10x the assumed publishing rate this is 230 GB/year, costing GBP 3.45-5.75/month. At 1/10th it is 2.3 GB/year. Object storage does not become a budget line anywhere in this range, and the decision to retain originals holds throughout.

notes: Retains the 3 MB original plus a 200 KB web-size and a 30 KB thumbnail. Discarding originals would cut this to 1.7 GB/year but makes larger derivatives permanently unrecoverable.

assumptions.name: inserts_per_day
assumptions.impact_if_wrong: linear on database growth

assumptions.name: avg_record_bytes
assumptions.impact_if_wrong: linear; recipes at ~4 KB dominate comments at ~0.5 KB

assumptions.name: index_overhead
assumptions.impact_if_wrong: indexes, tuple headers, page fill factor and dead-tuple slack

results.formula: bytes_per_day = inserts_per_day * avg_record_bytes * index_overhead ; bytes_per_year = bytes_per_day * 365
results.calculation: bytes_per_day = 200 * 2048 * 2.5 = 1024000 bytes = 1.0 MB ; bytes_per_year = 1.0 * 365 = 365 MB = 0.37 GB

sensitivity.explanation: The smallest managed relational plan offers 10 GB. At the assumed rate that is 25 years of headroom; at 10x it is 2.5 years. The smallest plan is correct across the entire plausible range, and storage is not what will force an upgrade - the connection limit is more likely to bind first.

assumptions.name: avg_rps
assumptions.impact_if_wrong: linear on egress

assumptions.name: avg_payload_bytes
assumptions.impact_if_wrong: linear; blended from 60% image requests at ~80 KB and 40% HTML/JSON at ~15 KB

assumptions.name: origin_egress_price
assumptions.impact_if_wrong: linear on cost; price table dated 2026-08-09

results.formula: egress_per_month = avg_rps * avg_payload_bytes * 2592000 ; cost = origin_gb * origin_price

sensitivity.explanation: This is the number that decides whether a CDN is justified, and it is the one a photo-sharing brief makes people assume is large. 3.9 GB/month is 0.4% of the ~1 TB/month threshold at which edge offload repays its complexity point. Even at 20x - 78 GB/month, GBP 3-7 - a CDN saves single-digit pounds and costs a component. The decision does not change anywhere in the plausible range.

notes: Uses average RPS, not peak: egress is billed on volume. Billing at peak would overstate this by 10x.

assumptions.name: arrival_rate
assumptions.impact_if_wrong: linear on concurrency

assumptions.name: service_time_ms
assumptions.impact_if_wrong: linear; a rendered recipe page with a small number of indexed queries

assumptions.name: target_utilisation
assumptions.impact_if_wrong: operating point, not conservatism: waiting time grows non-linearly above ~0.7

results.formula: L = arrival_rate * service_time_seconds ; provisioned = L / target_utilisation

result.unit: mean concurrent in-flight requests at peak

safety_margin.rationale: Sized to 65% utilisation rather than 100%. At rho=0.9 waiting time is roughly 10x service time and at rho=0.95 roughly 20x, so the headroom is an operating point rather than caution.

sensitivity.explanation: Required concurrency is 0.05. Service time would have to be roughly 2000x higher - four minutes per request - before one instance's worth of concurrency became the constraint. Horizontal scaling and load balancing have no measured problem to solve.

assumptions.name: queries_per_request
assumptions.impact_if_wrong: linear on concurrent queries; irrelevant because the pool floor dominates

assumptions.name: query_time_ms
assumptions.impact_if_wrong: linear

assumptions.name: instances
assumptions.impact_if_wrong: one web process plus one scheduled task process

assumptions.name: safety
assumptions.impact_if_wrong: Little's Law gives the mean; pools must absorb the tail

assumptions.name: min_pool
assumptions.impact_if_wrong: a pool sized to the mean queues on acquisition during any burst

results.formula: concurrent = query_rate * query_time_seconds ; pool_per_instance = max(min_pool, ceil(concurrent / instances * safety)) ; total = instances * pool_per_instance
results.calculation: query_rate = 0.28 * 5 = 1.4 queries/s ; concurrent = 1.4 * 0.004 = 0.0056 ; pool_per_instance = max(5, ceil(0.0056 / 2 * 4)) = max(5, 1) = 5 ; total = 2 * 5 = 10

sensitivity.dominant_input: the database plan's max_connections, not any traffic input
sensitivity.explanation: Demand is set by the pool floor, not by load: 10 connections regardless of whether traffic is 0.01 or 4 req/s. What varies is the limit. The smallest managed plans often cap max_connections around 20-25, where 10 connections is already 40-50% of the limit - the first resource on the smallest plan likely to bind, ahead of CPU or storage. A separate connection pooler is still unjustified, since the threshold is 80% of the limit.

assumptions.name: read_rate
assumptions.impact_if_wrong: linear on what a cache would relieve

assumptions.name: hottest_key_share
assumptions.impact_if_wrong: the browse/home listing is the single most-requested view

assumptions.name: hit_rate
assumptions.impact_if_wrong: generous for a listing that changes whenever anyone publishes

results.formula: hottest_key_rate = read_rate * hottest_key_share ; relieved = hottest_key_rate * hit_rate
results.calculation: hottest_key_rate = 0.27 * 0.3 = 0.081 req/s ; relieved = 0.081 * 0.5 = 0.041 queries/s removed from a database serving 1.4 queries/s

sensitivity.explanation: The threshold below which a cache is not justified is roughly 10 requests/second on a single key. The hottest key here runs at 0.081 req/s - 123x below it. Even if one key took 100% of reads at the high traffic extreme, it would be 4.2 req/s, still under the threshold. A cache would remove 0.04 queries/second from a database doing 1.4. There is no measured problem for it to solve.

assumptions.name: arrival_rate
assumptions.impact_if_wrong: 20 photos/day plus a handful of notification emails

assumptions.name: service_time_seconds
assumptions.impact_if_wrong: decode and resize a 3 MB photo twice

assumptions.name: target_utilisation
assumptions.impact_if_wrong: queue depth grows without bound as utilisation approaches 1

results.formula: workers = ceil(arrival_rate * service_time_seconds / target_utilisation) ; capacity = workers / service_time_seconds ; drain_time = backlog / (capacity - arrival_rate)
results.calculation: workers = ceil(0.00023 * 3 / 0.7) = ceil(0.00099) = 1 ; capacity = 1 / 3 = 0.33 jobs/s ; drain_time(100 jobs) = 100 / (0.33 - 0.00023) = 303 s = 5.1 minutes

sensitivity.explanation: One worker is 1400x over-provisioned for the assumed arrival rate, and a 100-job backlog drains in about 5 minutes. Arrival would have to reach roughly 0.23 jobs/second - 1000x the assumption - before a second worker was needed, and roughly 500 jobs/second before a dedicated broker was justified over a jobs table in the existing database. The stronger finding is that resizing in the browser removes this work entirely, so the queue exists only for notification email and cleanup.

components.name: Application runtime (single managed web instance)
components.justification: Peak demand is 0.28 requests/second and 0.034 mean concurrent in-flight requests. One small instance at a conservatively-assumed 10 req/s capacity is 36x peak, and 2.4x the extreme end of the sensitivity range (4.2 req/s). Serves HTML/JSON, issues pre-signed upload URLs, and runs a scheduled task from the same codebase and deployment that drains the jobs table.

components.name: Relational database (managed, smallest tier, automated backup with point-in-time recovery)
components.justification: Users, recipes, ingredients, steps, comments and tags are strongly related entities and the query patterns are not yet known, which is exactly the case relational is the default for. Peak writes are 0.014/second and storage grows 0.37 GB/year, so the smallest plan has 25 years of headroom. Also carries the full-text search index and the jobs table, avoiding two further components.

components.name: Object storage (managed, public-read for derivatives, versioning enabled)
components.justification: Photos grow 23 GB/year at GBP 0.35-0.58/month and are served directly to browsers, keeping 3.9 GB/month of image egress off the application instance entirely. Versioning is a bucket setting, costs nothing, and makes an accidental delete of irreplaceable user content recoverable.

components.name: Error tracking (managed, free tier at this volume)
components.justification: Error tracking is a scale-independent fundamental: its failure is not proportional to traffic, so a small system gets no discount. At 2,400 requests/day the event volume sits inside every vendor's free tier. This is the fourth point and it is what puts the design at 4/4 - included deliberately rather than traded away for a headroom figure.

rejected_components.reason: Origin egress is 3.9 GB/month, costing GBP 0.16-0.35. Edge offload does not repay its complexity point below a few hundred GB/month. A photo-sharing brief makes a CDN feel mandatory; the arithmetic puts this at 0.4% of the ~1 TB/month threshold. If the chosen object storage provider bundles edge delivery as a bucket setting rather than a separate distribution to configure and invalidate, take it - that is 0 points.
rejected_components.revisit_when: Origin egress exceeds 500 GB/month for 2 consecutive months (trigger egress-volume), or a material user segment reports cross-region p95 above 150 ms.

rejected_components.reason: The hottest single key runs at 0.081 requests/second against a ~10 req/s threshold - 123x below it. A cache would remove 0.041 queries/second from a database serving 1.4 queries/second at low single-digit utilisation. It would add a component, a staleness class, and an invalidation question on every write path in exchange for nothing measurable.
rejected_components.revisit_when: Any single query exceeds 100 executions/minute at p95 above 50 ms (trigger hot-query-rate). Check the query's index first - a cache over an unindexed query is a latency landmine.

rejected_components.reason: Job arrival is 0.00023/second. A jobs table in the existing database costs 0 points, is atomic with the business write so there is no dual-write problem to solve with an outbox, and is inspectable with SQL during an incident. A managed queue would reintroduce the dual-write problem the database table avoids by construction.
rejected_components.revisit_when: Sustained job throughput above 500 jobs/second at peak over a week, or the jobs table measurably competing with application queries for connections and I/O.

rejected_components.reason: There are no independent consumer groups and no replay requirement. Event rate would be 0.00023/second against a threshold of roughly 500/second, and streaming is stage-4 machinery against a stage-1 system.
rejected_components.revisit_when: Three or more independent consumers need to replay the same stream - which is a structural requirement, not a volume one.

rejected_components.reason: The work it would exist to do is 20 image resizes per day. Resizing in the browser before upload removes the work entirely, cuts the mobile upload payload from 3 MB to 200 KB, and keeps image decoding of untrusted input out of the server process. What async work remains - notification email, orphaned-upload cleanup - is drained by a scheduled task on the existing application.
rejected_components.revisit_when: Oldest pending job age exceeds 15 minutes after a normal spike has passed, twice in a month (trigger async-job-backlog), or the platform turns out to bill scheduled tasks as a separate always-on process.

rejected_components.reason: Full-text search over roughly 2,400 recipes at the end of year one is sub-millisecond with a generated tsvector column and a GIN index in the database already being run. A separate search engine is a second datastore technology (+1 point on top of its own point) with no stated requirement it uniquely meets.
rejected_components.revisit_when: Search p95 exceeds 300 ms after the index is confirmed in use, or a stated requirement for relevance ranking, typo tolerance or faceting that the database provably cannot meet.

rejected_components.reason: The primary serves 1.4 queries/second at low single-digit CPU utilisation. A replica would add a component, a second connection target, and replication lag - which makes reading from it a correctness decision, not only a performance one.
rejected_components.revisit_when: Primary database CPU sustained above 70% for 3 days after query optimisation (trigger db-cpu-sustained).

rejected_components.reason: Demand is 10 connections, set by the pool floor rather than by load. A separate pooler is justified above roughly 80% of max_connections; 10 connections against a limit of 20-25 on the smallest plans is 40-50%. It would add a hop, a process, and a failure mode.
rejected_components.revisit_when: Connections used exceed 80% of max_connections, sustained 1 hour and recurring (trigger db-connections). Note this is the resource on the smallest plan most likely to bind first.

rejected_components.reason: One instance runs at roughly 3% of a conservatively-assumed capacity at peak. A load balancer's value here would be redundancy rather than distribution, and redundancy without a second instance and a database that fails over automatically buys very little.
rejected_components.revisit_when: An availability target above ~99.5% is actually stated and funded (see the availability section - it is not reachable inside GBP 50/month), or instance CPU sustained above 70% for 3 days.

rejected_components.reason: One deployable unit, two developers, no dedicated operations capacity. A self-managed orchestration platform is 4 points on its own - the entire available budget - to run a single process.
rejected_components.revisit_when: More independently deployable services than the team can run by hand, with dedicated operations capacity funded. Neither condition is close.

rejected_components.reason: Recipes have meaningful relationships to users, ingredients, tags and comments, transactions span entities, and the query patterns are not yet known - joins let new questions be asked without remodelling. Adding it alongside the relational store would cost a point for the component and another for the additional datastore technology.
rejected_components.revisit_when: Access becomes genuinely whole-document-by-id with per-record variable shape. A variable region within an otherwise structured record is better served by a JSON column in the relational store.

rejected_components.reason: A single-timezone audience with no latency or availability requirement that one region provably cannot meet. Multi-region for a stateful component is 4 points - the whole budget - and stage-5 machinery against a stage-1 system.
rejected_components.revisit_when: Cross-region p95 above 150 ms for a material user segment, sustained.

options.description: The simplest viable option. One managed application instance, one managed relational database, one object storage bucket, managed error tracking. Photos are uploaded to the application, resized server-side inside the request, and written to object storage. No worker, no queue, no CDN, no cache.
options.reason: Rejected on the resize duration, not on capacity - the capacity case for it is sound. A 3 MB phone photo decoded and resized twice is roughly 3 seconds inside a request the user is waiting on, on a shared-CPU instance, with image decoding of untrusted input running in the web process. The measurement that would change the answer: if p95 server-side resize time for representative phone photos is under ~300 ms, the synchronous path is comfortably within a normal request budget and this becomes the correct answer, since it is otherwise identical to the selected option and involves less client code.
trade_offs: Identical component count and cost to the selected option; the difference is entirely in where the work happens
Simpler client: a plain multipart form upload with no JavaScript dependency
3 MB uploads over mobile connections, which is the slowest part of publishing a recipe
Image decoding of untrusted input inside the web process, a recurring vulnerability class
A resize failure fails the publish, and a process restart mid-resize loses the work with nothing to retry it

options.description: Selected. Same four components. Photos are resized in the browser and PUT directly to object storage via a short-lived pre-signed URL, so image bytes never traverse the application. The original is uploaded alongside the derivatives by the same mechanism. A jobs table in the existing database, drained by a scheduled task on the same application, handles notification email and orphaned-upload cleanup. Full-text search uses the database's own index.
trade_offs: No headroom: 4/4. Any addition requires removing something or adding an engineer
Client-side resize quality varies across browsers and devices, and users with JavaScript disabled cannot upload
A pre-signed URL accepts whatever the client sends, so content-type, content-length and expiry must be constrained in the policy and dimensions validated server-side from the image header
User-uploaded media must be served from a separate domain so a stored SVG or HTML payload cannot execute in the application's origin
One application instance and one database instance means deploys, database maintenance windows and restarts are user-visible; ~99.5% is what this delivers
A scheduled task draining a jobs table has coarser latency than a always-on worker - work waits up to the scheduling interval

options.description: The selected components plus a dedicated always-on worker process consuming the jobs table, generating image derivatives server-side after the upload returns.
options.reason: Over budget at 5/4, to serve a job arrival rate of 0.00023/second - one worker would be roughly 1400x over-provisioned. The measurement that would change the answer: sustained async job arrival above roughly 0.23 jobs/second, or oldest pending job age above 15 minutes twice in a month. Both are armed as triggers, and the second one fires before users notice.
trade_offs: Bounded upload latency without depending on client-side resize, and a real retry story for failed derivative generation
Costs the fifth point against an available four, and roughly GBP 240/month of engineering attention
Still requires 3 MB to reach either the application or the bucket, so it does not fix the mobile upload experience that client-side resize does
Keeps image decoding of untrusted input on the server, just out of the request path

options.description: The reflex architecture for a photo-sharing app: application instance, dedicated worker, managed relational database, object storage, CDN in front of media, managed queue, managed key-value cache, error tracking.
options.reason: 225% of the complexity budget and over the stated infrastructure budget before operational cost is counted - 9 points is roughly GBP 2,160/month of engineering attention against GBP 960 for the selected option. Every added component is below its own justification threshold by two to three orders of magnitude: egress 3.9 GB/month against ~1 TB for a CDN, hottest key 0.081 req/s against ~10 req/s for a cache, job arrival 0.00023/s against ~500/s for a broker. The measurement that would change the answer is any one of those three thresholds being crossed; each is armed as a separate trigger, so the components can be added individually when their own numbers justify them, rather than together on intuition.
trade_offs: Every component here is the right answer at some scale, and each has a defensible story in isolation
Overengineering is the accumulation, not any single decision - which is what the budget makes visible
The cache alone (GBP 30-70/month) exceeds the entire infrastructure budget's headroom
Two datastore technologies beyond the first, in a team of two with no dedicated operations capacity

options.description: A single small virtual machine running the application, a self-hosted relational database, and photos on local block storage, with managed error tracking. The cheapest invoice available. Scored 8: self-hosted stateless runtime 2, self-hosted stateful database 3, self-hosted media serving and its backups 2, managed error tracking 1.
options.reason: The cheapest invoice and the most expensive architecture. 8 points is roughly GBP 1,920/month of engineering attention against GBP 960 for the selected option, to save GBP 10-25/month on the invoice - a net cost of about GBP 950/month. Backup, point-in-time recovery, patching and restore testing become the team's responsibility, and backups on the same machine as the primary fail the one test that matters. The measurement that would change the answer: managed database cost exceeding roughly GBP 1,000/month, at which point the 3-point self-hosting premium starts to be repaid. Current managed cost is GBP 10-20/month.
trade_offs: Lowest invoice by a small margin, and full control over configuration and versions
Self-hosted stateful services are 3 points each; the model charges for on-call surface, not for instance count
Backups, PITR and a tested restore become work the team must do and keep doing - and these are scale-independent fundamentals that cannot be traded for simplicity
Photos on block storage cost GBP 0.08-0.12/GB against GBP 0.015-0.025 for object storage, so even the storage line is 4-5x more expensive

availability.explanation: No target was stated, and none has been invented. What this architecture realistically delivers is about 99.5% - roughly 3.6 hours/month - dominated by deploys, database maintenance windows, and restarts of the single application instance. Three serial managed dependencies at ~99.9% each give a ceiling of ~99.7% before any of this system's own code runs. Reaching 99.9% would need a second instance behind a health-checked load balancer and a database plan with automated failover; the smallest plans do not offer failover, so that means stepping up to a small managed relational plan (GBP 120-200/month) plus a standby, putting infrastructure at GBP 150-250/month - three to five times the stated budget. 99.9% is not reachable inside GBP 50/month, and that is a budget decision rather than an architecture one.

triggers.metric: application instance CPU utilisation at peak
triggers.action: Re-run capacity analysis with measured request rate and service time; profile the dominant endpoint before adding a second instance
triggers.notes: This is the real trigger behind the single-instance decision. The users-past-sensitivity-limit trigger is the proxy that works before anyone is watching a dashboard.

triggers.source: monthly review: SELECT count(*) FROM users, recorded in the team's monthly notes
triggers.action: Re-run the full capacity analysis with measured traffic; the single-instance assumption is the first thing to re-derive
triggers.notes: Derived: peak_rps = users * 0.002778, so 2,500 users projects to 6.9 req/s, which is 70% of the conservatively-assumed 10 req/s single-instance capacity. The roundness of 2,500 is a coincidence of the arithmetic, not a number chosen for comfort.

triggers.action: Identify the dominant query and confirm its index is in use; evaluate query optimisation before a larger plan or a read replica
Evaluate pool sizing against measured concurrency before considering a separate pooler; check for connections held across external calls
triggers.notes: Most likely of the database triggers to fire first. Demand is 10 connections set by the pool floor, and the smallest managed plans often cap max_connections around 20-25 - already 40-50%.

triggers.metric: database storage used as a share of plan capacity
triggers.action: Plan retention and archival for the jobs table and any log-like tables; size the next plan tier against measured growth
triggers.notes: 6 GB of a 10 GB plan. At 0.37 GB/year this is ~15 years away; at 10x the assumed write rate, ~18 months.

triggers.source: cloud provider billing and usage dashboard
triggers.action: Compute the cost of edge offload against current origin egress pricing and the measured static-asset share
triggers.notes: Half the ~1 TB/month threshold at which a CDN repays its point, so the analysis starts with runway rather than at the cliff. Current: 3.9 GB/month.

triggers.source: cloud provider usage dashboard, monthly review
triggers.action: Review whether 3 MB originals still need retaining at full resolution; evaluate lifecycle tiering against measured access patterns

triggers.metric: executions per minute and p95 duration for the single most-executed query
triggers.source: database statement statistics (pg_stat_statements or equivalent), reviewed monthly
triggers.window: sustained across a monthly review, not a single sample
triggers.action: Confirm the query's index is in use and the plan is what you expect; evaluate query optimisation before adding a cache
triggers.notes: This metric is NOT emitted by default. Enabling the statement-statistics extension is a prerequisite of this decision, not a follow-up - without it the trigger guarding the cache rejection can never fire.

triggers.metric: age of the oldest unprocessed job
triggers.source: internal admin page running SELECT max(now() - created_at) FROM jobs WHERE state = 'pending'
triggers.window: after a normal spike has passed, twice in one month
triggers.action: Re-run capacity analysis for the async subsystem; evaluate a dedicated always-on worker against measured job arrival and service time
triggers.notes: Requires the jobs table and the admin page; both are part of the build. Oldest job age rises before depth does when workers are undersized, which is why it is the metric rather than depth.

triggers.metric: successful requests / total requests against the recipe browse endpoint
triggers.source: external uptime check on the browse endpoint, free tier
triggers.action: Identify the dominant downtime source - deploys, database maintenance windows, or instance restarts - before adding redundancy; two of those three are addressable without a component
triggers.notes: The external check does not exist yet. Setting it up is part of this decision - measured from the user's perspective, not from instance uptime.

triggers.action: Identify the dominant line item and check it against the capacity numbers in this design; a line that has outgrown its projection is a signal the traffic assumptions were wrong

triggers.source: confirmed team composition at a quarterly review
triggers.action: Re-run the complexity budget; below two engineers the available budget floors at 3 and this design is over budget, so identify which component to remove or move further into a managed service
triggers.notes: The budget is a function of the team, not only of the architecture. A design at 4/4 goes over the moment one developer leaves - the usual candidate to drop is self-managed error tracking, or consolidating the scheduled task into the web process.

triggers.metric: days since the last successful, timed restore of the database into a scratch environment
triggers.source: the team's restore-test log; a date recorded manually after each test
triggers.action: Perform a restore into a scratch environment, record the elapsed time as the actual RTO, and compare it against what was assumed
triggers.notes: A restore test older than a quarter should be treated as no restore test. This trigger guards the one failure mode with no workaround, and it is scale-independent - 100 users losing their recipes is as total a failure as a million.

open_questions: Does the chosen application platform run a scheduled task from the same deployment, or does it bill a separate always-on process? If the latter, this design is 5/4 and something must come out. This is the single highest-value question to answer before picking a platform.

Does the smallest managed relational plan offer point-in-time recovery, or snapshot-only backups? The difference is an RPO of minutes versus up to 24 hours for irreplaceable user content, and it is a plan-selection criterion rather than an architecture change.

What is max_connections on the chosen plan? At 10 connections of demand, a limit of 20 puts the design at 50% on day one - this is the resource most likely to force a plan upgrade, ahead of CPU or storage.

Are recipes and photos public, or is per-user access control required? Private media means short-lived signed URLs for every image request rather than public-read object URLs. That is application work, not a new component, but it changes the media-serving design.

Is the audience in the UK or EU? No compliance requirements were stated, but data protection law applies to stored email addresses and user content regardless of whether it was mentioned. The architectural consequence is bounded - a working account-and-content deletion path that also removes objects from storage - but it is not zero and it is cheaper to build in than to retrofit.

What is the actual p95 duration of a server-side resize of a representative phone photo? Under ~300 ms and opt-single-app-server-side-resize becomes the better answer, since it is otherwise identical and needs less client code.

A single load test confirming one instance sustains 10 requests/second for the recipe browse page would validate the load-bearing assumption of this whole design for perhaps an hour of work. It is the cheapest available conversion of a low-confidence input into an observed one.
